questions.q: What does this lesson mean by describing its additions as "additive wrapping" around the Lesson 29 build?
options: The tool schemas and approval checkpoint logic from Lesson 29 are rewritten from scratch
Audit logging, stopping conditions, budgets, and credential scoping are added around the existing, working handle_tool_use logic without modifying that core logic itself
The entire capstone project is discarded and restarted
Lesson 30 removes the approval checkpoint built in Lesson 29
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a working, tested core shouldn't be disturbed just to add safety layers — every new control wraps around the existing handler rather than changing it.

questions.q: According to this lesson's audit-logging code, which calls should produce a log entry?
options: Only calls to issue_refund that get approved
Only calls that get rejected
Every call — approved, rejected, or ungated (like get_order) — should write one audit entry
No calls should be logged until the entire task completes
questions.explain: The entry is built and appended for every tool_use handled, regardless of whether it was gated, approved, or rejected — consistent with Lesson 21's guidance to log more than just successes.

questions.q: Why does this lesson use MAX_ITERATIONS = 8 and budget_usd = 0.50 instead of the larger numbers used as general examples in Lessons 23 and 24?
options: Because these are hard-coded values that must always be used for every agent

Because this specific refund-lookup task genuinely needs fewer iterations and less budget than an open-ended task, illustrating Lesson 24's point that budgets should be sized per task, not copy-pasted generically
Because the Claude API enforces these exact limits automatically
Because larger numbers are not technically supported by the API
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes these numbers are task-specific — a refund lookup is cheap and bounded, so its budget and iteration cap are set smaller than a general-purpose example would need.

questions.q: What does scoping the capstone's credential to scopes: ["refunds:write", "orders:read"] instead of ["*"] accomplish?
options: It makes the API calls run measurably faster

It applies least privilege so that even if every other control somehow failed, the credential itself cannot reach anything outside orders and refunds, such as account settings or stored payment methods
It has no real security benefit over a full-access key
It automatically generates the audit log entries
questions.explain: A scoped credential, per Lesson 25's least-privilege principle, structurally limits the worst-case damage regardless of what the agent's logic does or fails to do — a guarantee the full-access key wouldn't provide.

questions.q: If MAX_RECORDS_MODIFIED = 1 and the agent attempted to call issue_refund on a second, different order within the same task, what should happen according to this lesson's framing?
options: The second call should be allowed, since the budget only applies to cost, not to how many records are touched
The action-scope limit should stop the second call, since it would exceed the one-record limit for this task — the same stopping-condition pattern from Lesson 23/24 applied here
The entire audit log should be deleted and restarted
The agent's credentials should be upgraded to scopes: ["*"] to allow it
questions.explain: MAX_RECORDS_MODIFIED is exactly the kind of action-scope limit from Lesson 24 — it should stop a second record-modifying call from proceeding, since this task is scoped to touch exactly one order.
